problems.body: Four pieces, but are they quarters?

widget.prompt: A pizza is cut into 4 pieces. When is each piece a quarter (1/4)?

options.label: Only if the 4 pieces are EQUAL
options.feedback: A fraction's pieces must be fair — four equal shares. Four random slices are just… four slices.

options.label: Always — four pieces means fourths
options.feedback: Cut one giant slice and three slivers: still 4 pieces, but nobody calls a sliver a quarter. Equal is the rule.

options.label: Only if the pizza is round
options.feedback: Shape doesn't matter — square pans cut into 4 equal pieces make quarters too. EQUAL matters.

options.label: Never — pizzas can't be fractions
options.feedback: Anything you can cut fairly can be fractioned — pizzas, ribbons, hours. Four equal shares = fourths.

hints: Would the tiny one be 'a quarter'?
explanationVariants: Fourths means four EQUAL parts — equal is what makes a piece a quarter.
The bottom number counts fair shares, not just cuts.

widget.prompt: A ribbon is cut into 6 equal pieces. What fraction of the ribbon is ONE piece?

options.feedback: One piece out of six equal pieces — the bottom counts ALL the shares, the top counts yours.
6/1 is six WHOLE ribbons! The share-count sits on the bottom; your one piece rides on top.
Count every piece for the bottom number — the cut made six, not five (a classic cuts-vs-pieces slip: 5 cuts, 6 pieces).
6/6 is all six pieces — the whole ribbon. One piece is 1/6.

hints: How many equal pieces in all?
That count goes on the bottom.
explanationVariants: One of six equal pieces is 1/6 — bottom counts the shares, top counts yours.
Watch the cuts-vs-pieces trap: 5 snips make 6 pieces.

widget.prompt: How many fourths make one whole?

commonErrors.feedback: 1 is a single fourth — one piece. The WHOLE needs every piece: four of the four.
8 fourths would be TWO wholes. One whole uses exactly as many pieces as the cut made: four.

widget.fallbackFeedback: A whole cut into fourths has exactly… how many pieces?

hints: The whole was cut into fourths.
explanationVariants: Four fourths rebuild the whole: 4/4 = 1.
The bottom number tells you how many pieces the whole IS.

widget.prompt: Which is bigger: 3/8 or 5/8 of the same cake?

options.feedback: Same-size pieces (eighths), so just compare counts: five pieces beat three.
Both fractions use eighth-size pieces — with piece size equal, MORE pieces is more cake: 5 > 3.

options.label: They're equal
options.feedback: The bottoms match (same piece size) but the tops don't — 5 pieces versus 3.

options.label: You can't compare fractions
options.feedback: Same cake, same piece size — this is just counting pieces: 5 beats 3.

explanationVariants: With equal piece sizes (same denominator), more pieces wins: 5/8 > 3/8.
Think stacks of identical blocks: a 5-stack beats a 3-stack.

widget.prompt: Which is bigger: 1/3 or 1/8 of the same sandwich?

options.feedback: Fewer cuts make BIGGER pieces — sharing with 3 people beats sharing with 8.
The trap! 8 is a bigger NUMBER, but it means more cuts — and more cuts make smaller pieces. Share with 3, eat more.

options.label: They're equal
options.feedback: Only the tops match. The bottoms set the piece SIZE: thirds are big, eighths are small.

options.label: You can't tell
options.feedback: Same sandwich, one piece each — the piece from the 3-way split is plainly bigger.

hints: The bottom number counts the sharers.
3 sharers or 8 — whose piece is bigger?
explanationVariants: 1/3 > 1/8: a bigger bottom number means MORE cuts and SMALLER pieces.
Would you rather split a sandwich with 2 friends or with 7?

widget.prompt: A chocolate bar has 6 equal pieces. You eat 1. How many SIXTHS are left?

commonErrors.feedback: 1 is the piece you ATE. The bar keeps the rest: 6 − 1 sixths.
6 sixths is the untouched bar — one of them is gone now.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Six pieces minus the one eaten.

explanationVariants: 6/6 minus 1/6 leaves 5/6 — five sixths still in the wrapper.
Eaten + left always rebuilds the whole: 1 + 5 = 6 sixths.

widget.prompt: A number line from 0 to 1 is split into 4 equal jumps. Where does 1/4 sit?

options.label: At the first jump mark after 0
options.feedback: One jump of the four — a quarter of the way along.

options.label: At the number 4
options.feedback: 4 is far past 1! The 4 in 1/4 counts the JUMPS between 0 and 1, not a place on the line.

options.label: A quarter of the way past 1
options.feedback: 1/4 is less than 1 — it lives between 0 and 1, at the first of the four marks.

options.label: At the fourth mark
options.feedback: The fourth mark is 4/4 — that's 1, the whole trip. 1/4 is one jump in.

hints: The trip from 0 to 1 takes 4 equal jumps.
explanationVariants: 1/4 sits one jump along a four-jump trip from 0 to 1.
Count the marks: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, then 4/4 lands exactly on 1.

widget.prompt: 3/3 of a sandwich is how many whole sandwiches?

commonErrors.feedback: 3 would be three whole sandwiches — that's 3/1, or 9/3. Three THIRDS is just all the pieces of one.
Zero would be no pieces at all (0/3). Three of the three pieces is everything — the whole sandwich.

hints: The sandwich was cut into 3 pieces.
explanationVariants: 3/3 = 1 whole — top equals bottom means every piece is present.
Any fraction with matching top and bottom (2/2, 5/5, 8/8) is exactly one whole.

widget.prompt: Which fraction equals exactly one whole?

options.feedback: Five of the five pieces — every share present, the whole rebuilt.
One piece of five — a small slice of the whole, not all of it.
5/1 means five WHOLES — five times too much. One whole is when top and bottom match.
Zero pieces taken — that's nothing at all, the opposite end from the whole.

hints: When does the top count ALL of the bottom's pieces?
explanationVariants: 5/5 = 1: the top counts every piece the bottom made.
The n/n family (2/2, 3/3, 4/4…) all land on the same spot: 1.

widget.prompt: A garden is split into 8 equal beds. 3 beds grow tomatoes. How many beds do NOT?

commonErrors.feedback: 3 is the tomato count — the question asks for the others.
8 is every bed. Take the 3 tomato beds away from the 8.

explanationVariants: 8 − 3 = 5 beds are tomato-free — that's 5/8 of the garden.
The garden splits into 3/8 tomatoes + 5/8 not: the parts always total 8/8.

widget.prompt: Two kids share a granola bar equally. What fraction does EACH get?

options.feedback: Two equal shares — each kid takes one of the two: a half.
Only two people are sharing — the bottom counts sharers, and there are 2, not 3.
2/1 is two whole bars each! The 2 belongs on the bottom (two shares); each kid's count on top is 1.
1/1 is the whole bar for one kid — the other gets crumbs. Equal sharing splits it: 1/2 each.

hints: That number goes on the bottom.
explanationVariants: Two equal shares → each is 1/2.
Sharing among n people always hands each person 1/n.

widget.prompt: Which is SMALLER: 1/6 or 1/2 of the same brownie?

options.feedback: Six-way sharing makes small pieces — 1/6 is a sliver next to a half.
A half is one of just TWO pieces — the big share. Six cuts make the smaller bits.

options.label: They're equal
options.feedback: The tops match but the bottoms don't — and the bottom sets piece size: sixths are much smaller than halves.

options.label: Neither can be smaller
options.feedback: One brownie, two ways to cut: the 6-way pieces are plainly smaller than the 2-way pieces.

explanationVariants: 1/6 < 1/2 — the bigger bottom number means smaller pieces.
Flip the question: which would you WANT? The half, obviously — so it's the bigger one.

widget.prompt: How many eighths make one whole?

commonErrors.feedback: 1 eighth is a single piece — the whole needs all of them.
4 eighths is only half the whole — four more pieces finish the job.

widget.fallbackFeedback: A whole cut into eighths holds exactly…?

explanationVariants: Eight eighths rebuild the whole: 8/8 = 1.
Halfway there is 4/8 — the other four complete it.

widget.prompt: Marta says: '1/4 of my small square equals 1/4 of your BIG poster.' Is she right?

options.label: Not necessarily — a fourth's size depends on the whole it comes from
options.feedback: Fractions describe a share OF something. A quarter of a poster dwarfs a quarter of a sticky note.

options.label: Yes — 1/4 always equals 1/4
options.feedback: The FRACTION is the same, but the AMOUNT isn't: 1/4 of an hour and 1/4 of a year are both fourths…

options.label: Her square's fourth is bigger
options.feedback: Her square is the SMALL one — its fourth is the smaller piece. Bigger whole, bigger fourth.

options.label: Fractions don't have sizes
options.feedback: They do once you name the whole: 1/4 of THIS poster is a real, measurable piece.

hints: A fraction is a share OF a whole.
explanationVariants: Same fraction, different wholes, different amounts — always ask 'a fourth of WHAT?'
1/4 of an elephant outweighs 4/4 of a mouse.

widget.prompt: A number line from 0 to 1 has 4 equal jumps. How many jumps land you on 3/4?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 jumps finish the whole trip — that's 4/4 = 1. Stop one jump earlier.
1 jump reaches 1/4. The top number counts your jumps: three of them.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The top number of 3/4 counts the jumps.

explanationVariants: Three jumps of one-fourth each land on 3/4.
The top number IS the jump count; the bottom sets the jump size.

widget.prompt: Which cut turns a chocolate bar into THIRDS?

options.label: 3 pieces, all the same size
options.feedback: Thirds = three EQUAL shares. Same size is the whole deal.

options.label: 3 pieces — one big, two tiny
options.feedback: Three pieces, yes, but unfair ones — the big chunk isn't 'a third,' it's just a chunk.

options.label: 2 equal pieces
options.feedback: Two equal pieces are halves. Thirds need one more fair cut.

options.label: 4 equal pieces
options.feedback: Equal, beautifully — but that's fourths. Thirds means exactly three fair shares.

hints: Thirds needs a specific count AND fairness.
How many pieces? Are they equal?
explanationVariants: Thirds = exactly 3 pieces, all equal — both conditions or it isn't thirds.
The name comes from the count: THREE fair shares, each one-third.

widget.prompt: How many thirds are in 2 whole pies?

commonErrors.feedback: 2 is the pie count. EACH pie holds 3 thirds — two pies hold more.
3 thirds is just ONE pie. The second pie brings 3 more.

explanationVariants: Each pie carries 3 thirds, so 2 pies carry 6: 6/3 = 2.
Whole numbers wear fraction costumes too — 2 = 6/3.

widget.prompt: Ana ate 4/6 of her sandwich; Ben ate 5/6 of his. The sandwiches are the same size. Who ate more?

options.label: Ben
options.feedback: Same wholes, same piece size (sixths) — just count: 5 pieces beat 4.

options.label: Ana
options.feedback: Both ate sixth-size pieces of equal sandwiches — Ben took one MORE piece: 5 > 4.

options.label: They ate the same
options.feedback: The bottoms match but the tops differ — one extra sixth separates them.

options.label: Impossible to know
options.feedback: Everything matches except the counts — and 5 > 4 settles it.

explanationVariants: With wholes and piece sizes equal, more pieces = more eaten: 5/6 > 4/6.
Ben left 1/6; Ana left 2/6 — the leftovers tell the same story.

widget.prompt: In 3/4, what does the BOTTOM number tell you?

options.label: How many equal parts the whole was cut into
options.feedback: The 4 sets the piece size: fourths. It's the cut-count.

options.label: How many parts you take
options.feedback: Taking is the TOP number's job (3). The bottom describes the cutting.

options.label: The answer to the fraction
options.feedback: A fraction isn't a problem to solve — it's a description: 3 pieces of a 4-piece cut.

options.label: Which number is bigger
options.feedback: Position, not size, gives the meaning: bottom = cut, top = take.

explanationVariants: Bottom = how the whole was cut (fourths); top = how many pieces you're counting (3).
Read 3/4 as a sentence: 'three of the four equal parts.'

widget.prompt: A pie is cut into 4 equal pieces. Grandpa takes 1 piece, then you take 1 more. How many FOURTHS are taken?

commonErrors.feedback: 1 counts only one taker — Grandpa's piece AND yours are both gone.
4 fourths would be the whole pie — two pieces still sit in the tin.

explanationVariants: 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4 — two of the four pieces are taken.
Two remain: taken (2) + left (2) = 4/4, the whole pie.

widget.prompt: Same cake, different shares. Sort each against one half.

items.feedback: Half of 4 pieces is 2 — and 3 beats 2. Three-fourths clears the half.
Half of 3 pieces would be 1½ — one piece falls short of half.
Half of 8 is 4 — five eighths is one piece past half.
Half of 6 is 3 — two sixths sits below the halfway line.

widget.missFeedback: Find half of each bottom number, then compare the top to it.
widget.successFeedback: 3/4 and 5/8 clear the half; 1/3 and 2/6 fall short — half-of-the-bottom is the fence.

hints: Half the bottom number is the fence.
Half of 4 is 2; half of 8 is 4…
Compare each top to its fence.
explanationVariants: A fraction beats 1/2 when its top beats half its bottom.
The half is a benchmark — most everyday comparisons only need it.

widget.prompt: A road from home (0) to school (1) has a marker at every fourth. Lea stands at the 2/4 marker. Where is she?

options.label: Exactly halfway to school
options.feedback: Two of four equal jumps — the same spot as 1/2. Two names, one place on the line.

options.label: Almost at school
options.feedback: Almost-there is 3/4, one marker further. 2/4 is only the middle.

options.label: Just leaving home
options.feedback: Just-leaving is 0 or 1/4. Two full jumps put her squarely in the middle.

options.label: Past the school
options.feedback: Past school would need a top bigger than the bottom (like 5/4). 2/4 is inside the trip.

hints: 2 out of 4 — what part of the trip?
explanationVariants: 2/4 of the way is the halfway point — 2 is half of 4.
Different fractions can name the SAME spot: 2/4 and 1/2 share it.

widget.prompt: How many quarters (fourths) are in 3 whole pizzas?

commonErrors.feedback: 3 counts PIZZAS. Each one splits into 4 quarters — the quarters multiply.
7 added 3 + 4. Three pizzas of 4 quarters each is a groups problem: 3 × 4.

explanationVariants: 3 pizzas × 4 quarters = 12 quarters — so 3 = 12/4.
Fractions meet multiplication: equal groups of pieces.

widget.prompt: Tomas says: '1/8 is bigger than 1/3, because 8 is bigger than 3.' What's wrong?

options.label: The 8 counts CUTS, not size — more cuts make smaller pieces
options.feedback: The bottom number splits the whole further. Eight-way sharing leaves slivers; three-way leaves slabs.

options.label: Nothing — Tomas is right
options.feedback: Picture both: a bar cut into 8 vs the same bar cut into 3. Which single piece would you grab? The third.

options.label: He should have added the numbers
options.feedback: Adding tops and bottoms mixes their jobs. The fix is knowing what the bottom MEANS: cuts.

options.label: Fractions with 8 don't exist
options.feedback: Eighths are perfectly real — just small. That's exactly the point.

hints: What does the bottom number do to the whole?
explanationVariants: The bigger denominator loses: 8 cuts make smaller pieces than 3 cuts — 1/8 < 1/3.
The big-number reflex is whole-number thinking; the bottom of a fraction works in reverse.

widget.prompt: A sub sandwich is cut into 8 equal parts for 8 kids. How many EIGHTHS does each kid get?

commonErrors.feedback: 8 eighths is the whole sub for one lucky kid — and seven hungry friends. Equal sharing hands out one piece each.
Zero would leave everyone hungry with the sub sitting there — each kid takes exactly one piece.

explanationVariants: 8 pieces shared by 8 kids = 1 eighth each: everyone holds 1/8.
Fair shares are division wearing a fraction costume: 8 ÷ 8 = 1 piece each.

widget.prompt: What is 0/4 of a cake?

options.label: Nothing — zero of the four pieces
options.feedback: A perfectly legal fraction meaning 'none of the shares': an empty plate.

options.label: The whole cake
options.feedback: The whole is 4/4 — every piece. Zero pieces is the other extreme.

options.label: Four pieces
options.feedback: The top says how many you take — and it says zero. The 4 only describes the cutting.

options.label: It can't exist
options.feedback: It exists fine: the cake got cut, you just took none. 0/4 = 0.

explanationVariants: 0/4 = 0: the cutting happened, the taking didn't.
The top slides from 0/4 (nothing) up to 4/4 (everything).

widget.prompt: Counting by thirds — 1/3, 2/3, then the whole. How many thirds IS the whole?

commonErrors.feedback: 1 third is the first step of the count — two more steps reach the whole.
4 thirds steps PAST the whole into a second pie. The whole lands exactly at 3.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The count reaches the whole when top meets bottom.

hints: The next step fills the whole.
explanationVariants: 1/3, 2/3, 3/3 — the whole is three thirds.
On the number line the thirds-count hits 1 exactly at 3/3.

widget.prompt: Two ribbons are the same length. Red is cut into 6 equal bits; blue into 3 equal bits. Which bits are LONGER?

options.label: The blue bits
options.feedback: Three-way cutting makes bigger pieces than six-way — fewer shares, longer bits.

options.label: The red bits
options.feedback: Red got MORE cuts — six shares from the same length must each be shorter.

options.label: Same length bits
options.feedback: Same ribbon length split 6 ways vs 3 ways — the 3-way pieces are twice as long.

options.label: Can't tell without measuring
options.feedback: Equal ribbons make it pure logic: fewer pieces from the same whole = longer pieces.

hints: Same wholes — only the cut counts differ.
explanationVariants: Blue's thirds beat red's sixths — fewer cuts of the same whole leave longer pieces.
Each blue bit equals two red bits laid end to end.

widget.prompt: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices; you take 5. Build the fraction of the pizza you took.

commonBuilds.feedback: 8/5 puts the cut-count on top — that's more than a whole pizza! The taking (5) rides on top; the cutting (8) sits below.
3/8 is what's LEFT in the box. The question asks what you TOOK: five of the eight.

widget.missFeedback: Top = pieces you took (5); bottom = pieces the cut made (8).
widget.successFeedback: 5/8 — five taken of eight cut. (The 3/8 left behind completes the whole.)

hints: Take on top, cut on the bottom.
explanationVariants: You took 5 of the 8 slices: 5/8.
Taken (5/8) + left (3/8) = 8/8 — the whole pizza, accounted for.

widget.prompt: A trail is 1 mile long, with a water stop at every SIXTH of a mile. After the 4th stop, how much trail is LEFT?

options.label: 2/6 of a mile
options.feedback: Six sixths total, four walked — two sixths remain.

options.label: 4/6 of a mile
options.feedback: 4/6 is the part already WALKED. The question asks for what's ahead: 6 − 4 sixths.

options.label: 2 miles
options.feedback: The whole trail is only 1 mile — what's left is a part of it, not double it.

options.label: 1/2 of a mile
options.feedback: Half would be 3 sixths left — but the 4th stop is already past halfway. Only 2 sixths remain.

explanationVariants: After 4 of the 6 sixths, 2/6 of a mile remains — walked + left = 6/6.
The 4th stop sits past the halfway mark (3/6), so less than half remains.
